nodes.title: Frostman inequalities
nodes.statement: For compact K⊂ℂ with positive capacity, UμK(z)≤V(K)=−log cap K on all of ℂ and UμK(z)=V(K) quasi-everywhere on K.
hypotheses: K is compact and cap K>0.
proofSteps: Variation toward a probability on a nonpolar potential sublevel contradicts minimality. Mutual-energy finiteness is supplied by strict-energy, so the variation has no undefined infinity subtraction.
Finite energy ignores the resulting polar exceptional set. Lower semicontinuity and the equilibrium integral equality then give UμK≤V(K) on the support.

The nearest-support-point argument of Levenberg Proposition 1.4 bounds the upper limit from outside the support by the support supremum. On a ball separated from the compact support, the translated planar kernels and their first two derivatives have uniform bounds; differentiating their finite-measure integral gives a real harmonic potential, using the native harmonic kernel. At infinity the unit mass gives U(z)=−log|z|+o(1). If a component had a value above V(K), the boundary upper-limit bound and the decay at infinity would place an attained maximum in its interior. The native strong harmonic maximum principle makes the potential constant on that component, contradicting its boundary limit (or its decay on the unbounded component). Hence the bound holds everywhere.
acceptance: For compact K⊂ℂ with positive capacity, UμK(z)≤V(K)=−log cap K on all of ℂ and UμK(z)=V(K) quasi-everywhere on K.

Uniqueness is proved in weighted-equilibrium, not assumed here.

nodes.title: Weighted zero-distribution criterion

Monic real polynomials Pi, of degrees ni→∞, with every root in K and ||Pi||K,wμ,ni^(1/ni)→1 have root laws converging weakly to μ. For a circle of radius R larger than |K|, the circle average of each probability potential is −log R, obtained by the uniformly convergent expansion of log(1−x/z). Hence the nonnegative continuous function Uν−Uμ has zero average on every such circle and is zero there.

The exterior power series then identifies every real polynomial moment of ν and μ. Real polynomials separate points of K; native Stone–Weierstrass implies equality of measures. Every weak cluster point is μ, and compactness yields convergence of the full sequence. No general complex zero-distribution or weighted norm-conversion theorem is needed.

nodes.title: Monic Chebyshev polynomials on real compact sets
nodes.statement: For nonpolar compact real K and r≥1, Tr is the unique monic real degree-r polynomial minimizing the uniform norm on K. It has r+1 alternating extremal points. Its roots are simple and real in the convex hull of K; each gap of K contains at most one root. For a finite interval set there is C>0 with cap(K)^r≤||Tr||K≤C cap(K)^r.
hypotheses: K real compact and nonpolar; positive degree for alternation; finite interval K for the uniform capacity bound.
proofSteps: Coefficient bounds from interpolation give existence. The alternation criterion gives uniqueness, simple real roots in the convex hull, and at most one root in each gap.

For finite interval K put tn=||Tn||K and Kn={x∈ℝ:|Tn(x)|≤tn}. Alternation places its bands inside the convex hull of K. The explicit pullback of interval equilibrium has density |Tn′|/(nπsqrt(tn²−Tn²)) on the bands. The finite-interval density construction, or the same Cauchy-transform argument, identifies it as μKn and gives mass 1/n per band and cap Kn=(tn/2)^(1/n). Each gap of K meets at most one band, so μKn(gap)≤1/n (CSZ Theorems 2.2–2.4). Let GK=V(K)−UμK. Since UμKn is constant on K⊂Kn, reciprocal integration gives ∫GK dμKn=log(cap Kn/cap K). The finite-interval continuous potential makes GK zero on K and bounded on each gap. Thus n∫GK dμKn≤Σgaps max GK, and tn≤2exp(Σgaps max GK)cap(K)^n. The lower bound follows from Frostman reciprocity against the polynomial root law. No general harmonic-measure representation or Parreau–Widom theory is required.
acceptance: For nonpolar compact real K and r≥1, Tr is the unique monic real degree-r polynomial minimizing the uniform norm on K. It has r+1 alternating extremal points. Its roots are simple and real in the convex hull of K; each gap of K contains at most one root. For a finite interval set there is C>0 with cap(K)^r≤||Tr||K≤C cap(K)^r.

nodes.title: Finite interval equilibrium density and Hölder bound
nodes.statement: For a finite interval set K, the equilibrium law is 1/2-Hölder. For 0<a<b, its interval potential at 0 is −log((a+b+2sqrt(ab))/4). The proof uses the finite-gap density |∏(x−cj)|/(πsqrt(|∏(x−aj)(x−bj)|)), with one cj in each gap fixed by vanishing gap integrals.
hypotheses: K finite interval set; 0<a<b for the exterior single-interval potential.
proofSteps: Write R(z)=∏i(z−ai)(z−bi). Choose the unique monic p of degree k−1 with ∫bi^a(i+1) p(x)/sqrt(|R(x)|) dx=0 in every gap. The homogeneous period matrix is invertible: a nonzero polynomial of degree≤k−2 with zero integral in each of k−1 disjoint gaps has a zero in every gap, a degree contradiction. The same sign argument gives exactly one simple zero ci of p in each gap.

Use the branch sqrt(R(z))~z^k on ℂ minus the interval union and put H=p/sqrt R. Its opposite boundary values across each interval have jump −2i|p(x)|/sqrt(|R(x)|). Cauchy–Goursat on a finite rectangle partition and the disk Cauchy formula deform the integral of H(ζ)/(ζ−z) to the two sides of the cuts. The endpoint arcs vanish by their O(r^(−1/2)) bound; the outer boundary vanishes as its radius grows since H=1/z+O(1/z²). Hence H(z)=∫ρ(x)/(z−x)dx with ρ=|p|/(πsqrt(|R|)). The 1/z coefficient proves mass one; the branch signs give positivity.

On each component the other endpoint factors stay bounded away from zero, giving ρ≤C/√((x−ai)(bi−x)). Integration gives the 1/2-Hölder interval-mass bound. The Hölder-potential theorem yields a finite continuous potential. The real part of H vanishes on interval interiors, so the potential is constant on each component; its zero gap integrals identify these constants. A supported finite-energy competitor has mutual energy equal to this constant. Strict energy then proves minimality and uniqueness; infinite-energy competitors cannot improve it. This identifies the law with equilibrium without importing a general Green-function or Herglotz construction.
For the single interval use the existing normalized Chebyshev law and its explicit outside potential to evaluate the value at 0.
